quote: I have not come to call the righteous but sinners.
firstReading: Paul urges the Ephesians to live worthily of their calling through humility, gentleness, patience, and loving forbearance. They are to preserve the unity given by the Spirit, for the Church is one: one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father. Yet Christ bestows diverse graces and ministries so that the holy ones may be equipped and the Body may grow toward mature union with him.
psalmSummary: Psalm 19 praises the silent yet universal proclamation of creation. The heavens recount God’s glory, and the firmament declares the work of his hands. Day and night continually hand on this testimony, without ordinary speech or audible words. Nevertheless, their witness reaches throughout the earth. The psalm invites reverent attention to the Creator whose wisdom and splendor are made known through all he has fashioned.
gospelSummary: Jesus sees Matthew at the tax office and calls him to follow. Matthew responds by rising and becoming a disciple. At a meal in Matthew’s house, tax collectors and sinners gather with Jesus and his disciples. The Pharisees object to this association, but Jesus answers that the sick need a physician, not those who consider themselves well. He directs them to learn the meaning of God’s desire for mercy rather than sacrifice. Jesus reveals that his mission seeks sinners, summoning them to conversion and restored communion with God.
saintReflection: Saint Matthew, Apostle and Evangelist (Feast): Saint Matthew was called by Jesus while sitting at the tax office and became one of the Twelve Apostles. His call reveals the initiative of grace: Christ approaches a person regarded with suspicion and invites him into discipleship rather than leaving him defined by his past. At the meal that follows, Jesus explains his mission through the prophetic demand for mercy and his call to sinners (Matthew 9:9–13). The Gospel traditionally associated with Matthew presents Jesus as the fulfillment of Israel's Scriptures and the teacher whose authority requires a response of faith and obedience. The Sermon on the Mount joins purity of heart, forgiveness, prayer, and care for others within the life of God's Kingdom. His remembrance affirms the possibility of conversion and awakens gratitude for undeserved mercy, with the responsibility to put Christ's teaching into practice rather than merely admire it.
dailyPrayer:
Lord Jesus Christ, you looked upon Matthew with mercy and called him from the tax office into the fellowship of the apostles. Look upon us with that same merciful gaze. Deliver us from every sin that obscures your call and from every habit by which we resist conversion.

Grant us the humility, gentleness, patience, and charity commended by Saint Paul. Gather your Church into the unity that comes from your Spirit, and help each member receive the grace and service entrusted to him or her for the building up of your Body.

Teach us to rejoice in your mercy toward sinners, never withholding compassion from those whom you seek. Through the intercession of Saint Matthew, give us a faithful love for your Gospel, a pure heart in prayer, forgiveness toward those who wrong us, and readiness to obey all that you teach. May our lives bear witness that you have come to call sinners into repentance and communion with the Father. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
The readings reveal Christ as the merciful Lord who calls persons into communion and builds them into his one Body. Matthew’s summons begins with Christ’s initiative: Jesus sees, speaks, and calls. The disciple’s response is real and necessary, but it is awakened by grace. Mercy does not excuse sin or leave a person unchanged; it draws the sinner from alienation into repentance, discipleship, and table fellowship with the Lord.

Paul shows the ecclesial form of this grace. Those called by Christ are not gathered as isolated believers but are joined in one body, one faith, and one baptism. Christ gives different gifts and ministries for the Church’s growth into mature union with him. Psalm 19 widens this vision: all creation proclaims the glory of God, preparing hearts to recognize the divine wisdom fully revealed in Christ. Saint Matthew’s remembrance therefore joins gratitude for forgiveness to obedient faith. To receive mercy is to learn mercy, to hear Christ’s teaching, and to live it within the communion of his Church.
exegesis:
Context: The Feast of Saint Matthew brings together a Gospel account of his call and Paul’s teaching on the Church’s unity and ministries. Matthew 9 belongs to a sequence in which Jesus manifests divine authority through teaching, healing, forgiveness, and the gathering of disciples. The call occurs with striking brevity. Jesus sees Matthew seated at the tax office, commands him to follow, and Matthew rises. The account does not dwell on explanations, preparation, or public rehabilitation. Its emphasis falls on Christ’s sovereign and merciful initiative and on the disciple’s concrete response. Jesus does not merely offer Matthew a different religious opinion; he summons him into personal discipleship and eventually into the apostolic company.

Context: The ensuing meal makes the meaning of the call visible. Tax collectors and sinners sit with Jesus and his disciples, provoking the Pharisees’ question. Their concern is not only social contact but religious holiness: how can one who claims to act for God share a table with those identified as sinners? Jesus responds with the image of a physician. His presence among sinners does not signify approval of sin; it reveals the saving purpose of his mission. He comes where the wound is, in order to heal. His appeal to the prophetic demand for mercy places the dispute within Israel’s Scriptures. Worship offered without merciful conformity to God’s own heart fails to grasp what sacrifice is meant to express.

Psalm: Psalm 19 moves from the proclamation of the heavens to the confession that God’s glory is made known everywhere. The sky and firmament do not speak through human language, yet their testimony extends across the earth. Their ordered beauty and continual witness direct creation toward its Maker. On this feast, the psalm also illuminates the apostolic vocation. The natural world announces God’s glory without words, while the apostles are sent to announce the Gospel through their preaching and lives. The psalm does not itself describe Matthew’s mission, but it provides a fitting liturgical horizon: the God whose glory creation declares is the God who, in Christ, calls and sends witnesses to the nations.

Gospel: Ephesians 4 begins with Paul’s appeal that believers live in a manner worthy of the calling they have received. This manner is marked by humility, gentleness, patience, and bearing with one another in love. Such virtues are not optional adornments to Christian life; they preserve the unity which the Holy Spirit has already given. Paul grounds this unity in the fundamental confession of the Church: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father. Baptismal incorporation into Christ therefore establishes a communion that precedes individual preference and calls believers to a persevering charity.

Gospel: Unity is not uniformity. Paul immediately speaks of grace given according to Christ’s gift and names ministries through which Christ serves and forms his Church: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers. Their purpose is the equipping of the holy ones for ministry and the building up of Christ’s Body. The goal is not merely outward organization but maturity: believers are to grow toward the fullness belonging to Christ. Saint Matthew’s apostolic calling may be read in this light. Called from his former occupation, he is not left simply as an object of mercy. He is incorporated into the apostolic foundation and serves the Church’s growth by witnessing to the Lord who called him.

Saints: Saint Matthew’s life, as supplied in the Church’s remembrance, directs attention to grace that meets a person in a compromised and distrusted position. Jesus does not leave Matthew defined by his past. He calls him, and Matthew follows. The Gospel traditionally associated with Matthew presents Jesus as the fulfillment of Israel’s Scriptures and as the authoritative teacher of the Kingdom. Its teaching joins inward conversion with visible obedience: purity of heart, forgiveness, prayer, and care for others belong together. Matthew’s feast thus guards against reducing mercy to sentiment. Divine mercy restores communion with God and makes possible a life ordered by Christ’s commands.

Today: The readings call the Church to receive Christ’s mercy with repentance and to extend that mercy faithfully. Christians may not assume the posture of those who judge themselves healthy while withholding compassion from others. Nor may they invoke mercy while refusing the transformation to which Christ calls them. The physician heals; the disciple rises and follows. In the Eucharistic assembly, the baptized are gathered as one Body despite diverse gifts and ministries. Humility, patience, and loving forbearance protect this communion. Through Saint Matthew’s intercession, the Church asks for grateful hearts that welcome sinners, confess the need for grace, and put the Lord’s teaching into practice so that his saving mercy may be made known.
